assessment: Early card selections and deck-building advice are our assessment of the rules text, not measured performance. Revisit them as games and results arrive.

sealed.intro: Opening a prerelease pool? Start with the cards you have: find two colours with enough early plays, answers, and ways to win. Use the archetypes to connect those cards, not to force a deck your pool cannot support.

steps.title: Lay out your options
steps.text: Sort your pool by colour. Separate broadly useful creatures and answers from cards that need a particular engine. Note your strongest threats, but compare the whole colour rather than choosing it for one rare.

steps.title: Compare two-colour decks
steps.text: Lay out the plausible pairs by mana cost. Which can affect the board early, answer a large creature or planeswalker, and still win a long game? A spectacular top end does not repair a deck with nothing to do in the first turns.

steps.title: Count support, not just payoffs
steps.text: For a graveyard deck, count ways to fill the graveyard. For artifact payoffs, count artifacts you can actually deploy. For Jace engines, count empower cards and creatures that can protect your planeswalkers.

steps.title: Make the mana work
steps.text: Prefer a reliable two-colour base. Consider a splash only when the payoff justifies it and your pool provides fixing; a double-coloured early spell is a poor splash. Room of Refuge fixes one chosen colour, while Heartwood only supplies red or green.

draft.intro: Preparing to draft? Learn the flexible cards first, then the support each colour pair needs. Use this guide to recognise options; a pick still depends on the pack, your curve, and the cards already in your pool.

steps.title: Begin with flexible cards
steps.text: Early in a draft, useful creatures and efficient answers leave more routes open than a narrow payoff. Compare a card's actual casting requirements, not just its colour or rarity.

steps.title: Look for repeated opportunities
steps.text: Several useful cards arriving in one colour are more informative than one late gold card. Keep checking whether a possible second colour provides the creatures and interaction your deck needs.

steps.title: Draft the missing pieces
steps.text: Once your plan is taking shape, count its enablers. A prepare payoff wants prepare spells; an artifact engine needs artifacts. Another payoff may help less than an early creature, removal spell, or fixing.

steps.title: Build for the games you must play
steps.text: Check your curve before adding another expensive spell. Avoid stretching the mana for every powerful card you see. Use the archetype notes to understand your deck's plan, then select the cards that make it happen.

mechanics.title: Empower Jace: build a resource you can spend
mechanics.text: Empower adds loyalty to one Jace token you control, creating one first if needed. A nontoken Jace does not count. The token offers −1 to surveil 1 or −3 to draw a card.
mechanics.tip: Plan both the activation and the defence: an exposed planeswalker can be attacked. Spending its last loyalty normally sends it to the graveyard.

mechanics.title: Prepare: the creature brings another spell
mechanics.text: A prepared permanent makes its prepare spell available as a copy in exile. Pay the spell's cost and respect its timing. Casting it unprepares the permanent; losing the permanent first loses the uncast copy.
mechanics.tip: Budget mana for both halves. When removal is likely, consider whether you can use the prepared spell before risking the creature.

mechanics.title: Heartwood: repeatable red or green mana
mechanics.text: A Heartwood is a red and green artifact token that taps for red or green mana. Unlike a Treasure, using its mana ability does not sacrifice it.
mechanics.tip: It supports expensive spells and artifact payoffs, but does not fix blue, black, or white. Check whether the effect that creates it says it enters tapped.

mechanics.title: Your graveyard is part of your hand
mechanics.text: Flashback gives a spell another use from the graveyard for its listed flashback cost; the spell is then exiled when it leaves the stack. Threshold checks for seven or more cards in your graveyard.
mechanics.tip: Do not double-count resources: flashing back a card can drop you below threshold. Twinned Vision also requires a discard when you use its flashback cost.

keyCards.why: Brings its own Heartwood and can turn artifacts into lasting growth plus protection or evasion.
keyCards.watch: Each activation costs one mana and another artifact. Keeping an artifact and mana available matters.

keyCards.why: Offers removal, mana, and a continuing source of cards or damage from one permanent.
keyCards.watch: Double red asks for a real red base. Four damage does not answer every threat; protect her from attacks.

keyCards.why: Can shrink a creature or turn a sacrifice into a trampling Beast, with more options on later turns.
keyCards.watch: Costs five mana including double black. The sacrifice mode also affects you; plan what you can give up.

keyCards.why: An early deathtouch creature can discourage attacks while empower adds a separate resource.
keyCards.watch: A useful defensive role does not make it a fast clock. Think about how your deck eventually wins.

keyCards.why: A flying creature plus a prepared token-making spell gives you multiple uses for one card.
keyCards.watch: The second spell costs mana and disappears if the creature leaves before you cast it.

keyCards.why: A 4/4 trampling token, then another through flashback, gives a green deck something to do in a long game.
keyCards.watch: The second cast costs six mana. Do not let this replace the early plays your deck needs.

keyCards.why: A creature with a built-in answer to an artifact or enchantment keeps a narrow effect useful in more games.
keyCards.watch: Its sacrifice ability is sorcery-speed; you cannot use it as a surprise during combat.

keyCards.why: Returns an inexpensive creature with an extra counter and offers a second use through flashback.
keyCards.watch: Needs a creature with mana value three or less in your graveyard. Check that your deck supplies enough targets.

keyCards.why: Offers a cheap spell now and another cast from the graveyard later, useful for spell-based plans.
keyCards.watch: The flashback cost includes discarding a card. Drawing two on that cast is not two free cards.

keyCards.why: Provides an early creature and a prepared self-mill spell to help reach threshold.
keyCards.watch: The threshold bonus needs seven graveyard cards. Outside a graveyard plan, compare it with your other early creatures.

keyCards.why: Its prepared spell can enable its own flying and haste, giving a burn-oriented deck a way to attack through a crowded board.
keyCards.watch: You need additional noncombat damage on later turns to keep enabling those abilities. Include the prepared spell's mana cost in your attack plan.

keyCards.why: Answers an opposing nonland permanent, including a planeswalker, rather than only a creature.
keyCards.watch: The permanent returns when this enchantment leaves. Consider opposing enchantment removal.

keyCards.why: Instant-speed exile handles creatures or planeswalkers and prevents ordinary graveyard recursion.
keyCards.watch: Four mana is a meaningful turn. Leave it up when the flexibility is worth delaying your own play.

keyCards.why: Two-mana instant interaction can remove a small creature or change combat by shrinking a larger one.
keyCards.watch: −3/−3 is not unconditional removal. Check toughness and possible protection or pump.

keyCards.why: Four damage at instant speed can answer a creature or planeswalker, with a discount when you control a legendary creature.
keyCards.watch: The discount is conditional and four damage has a ceiling.

keyCards.why: Adds a creature while offering a fight with another creature you already control.
keyCards.watch: Needs another suitable creature. Damage, deathtouch, and opposing removal can change whether the fight is favourable.

keyCards.why: Can protect a permanent, replace itself, or grow a creature before it fights.
keyCards.watch: The fight needs your creature to survive. The green-white cost is a commitment to both colours.

keyCards.why: Turns scrying or surveilling into an attack boost for your creatures; its prepared spell supplies a token and surveil.
keyCards.watch: Needs creatures to attack with and repeatable ways to trigger it. The boost triggers only once each turn.

keyCards.why: Can prepare again on your upkeep, offering repeated Heartwood production over several turns.
keyCards.watch: Each Soul Tether still costs mana. You need time and worthwhile uses for the extra mana or artifacts.

keyCards.why: Adds loyalty and rewards loyalty activations that remove two or more counters with an extra card.
keyCards.watch: A five-mana enchantment needs a stable board and suitable loyalty abilities. It does not stop an attack itself.

keyCards.why: A land that can supply your chosen colour, with a late-game use when you no longer need the mana.
keyCards.watch: Enters tapped and the colour is chosen once. Too many tapped lands can slow your opening turns.

keyCards.why: Produces any colour and can turn an unwanted card into a new draw later.
keyCards.watch: Costs three mana before it helps. It is not a substitute for enough lands of your main colours.

keyCards.why: Produces mana and turns later creatures entering into life-gain triggers.
keyCards.watch: A three-mana ramp creature can be inefficient when the deck has no life-gain rewards.

keyCards.why: Flying, trample and a cast trigger that untaps your lands offer a spectacular late play.
keyCards.watch: Both reviewers are sceptical: the mana investment is enormous, and an opponent may pay ward by sacrificing spare lands.

interactions.note: +2/+2 and flying can change a block; empower also leaves a resource behind.
Destroys any creature, but its controller draws if that creature was not attacking.
Flash: can give a permanent hexproof for the turn and add a counter to a creature or planeswalker.
Can tax a creature or legendary spell by three mana, or give a creature −5/−0 for the turn.
Usually needs an extra mana unless its behold-a-Jace additional cost is met. Read the full cost before planning a turn.
−3/−3 can kill outright or make a seemingly safe combat trade go badly.
Exiles a creature or planeswalker. A death trigger will not trigger just from being exiled.
Five damage, but only to a black or green creature or planeswalker. A matchup-specific answer.
Four damage to a creature or planeswalker; costs one mana less with a legendary creature in play.
Can give two +1/+1 counters and trample, or deal six damage to a flying creature.
Can protect a permanent with hexproof and indestructible, or add a counter before a fight.

exercises.question: You control a nontoken Jace planeswalker and no Jace tokens. You empower Jace 2. What happens?
options: Put two loyalty on the nontoken Jace
Create a Jace token and put two loyalty on it
Choose either option
exercises.explanation: Empower specifically checks for a Jace token. Your nontoken planeswalker does not meet that condition.

exercises.question: Your prepared Fatehold Chronologist leaves the battlefield before you cast Peer Review. Can you still cast that prepared copy?
options: Yes, until the end of the turn
Yes, whenever I can pay for it
No, the uncast copy ceases to exist
exercises.explanation: The prepared copy is tied to that permanent. This question is about a copy not yet cast, not a spell already on the stack.

exercises.question: You want to cast Silence the Echo without sacrificing a creature or planeswalker. With no cost-changing effects, how much mana do you need?
options: Two mana: one generic and one black
Five mana: four generic and one black
You cannot cast it without a sacrifice
exercises.explanation: The additional cost allows paying three mana instead of sacrificing. Add that to the printed cost of one generic and one black.

exercises.question: An undamaged 4/4 creature has no other relevant abilities or effects. You cast Last Gasp on it. What is it when the spell resolves?
options: A 1/1 until end of turn
A 4/4 with three damage marked
A creature with zero toughness
exercises.explanation: −3/−3 changes power and toughness. The creature is now 1/1 and does not die just from this effect.

exercises.question: You tap an untapped Heartwood for green mana using its printed mana ability. What happens to the token?
options: It is sacrificed like a Treasure
It stays on the battlefield, tapped
It becomes a Forest
exercises.explanation: Heartwood's mana ability has a tap cost, not a sacrifice cost. It can provide mana again after it untaps.

exercises.question: You control an empower Jace token but no legendary creatures. How much does Wrath of the Bloodmane cost?
options: Two mana: one generic and one red
Three mana: two generic and one red
One red mana
exercises.explanation: The discount needs a legendary creature. A Jace token is a planeswalker, so it does not meet that condition.

exercises.question: You have enough mana to flash back Twinned Vision, but no cards in hand. Can you cast it for its flashback cost?
options: Yes, drawing two pays for the discard
No, discarding a card is part of the cost
Yes, but you only draw one card
exercises.explanation: You must pay the discard before the spell resolves. The future draw cannot pay that cost.

exercises.question: Your only other artifact is an untapped Heartwood. With no floating mana or untapped lands, can it pay for Puppetbeast’s ability that grants hexproof?
options: No, a tapped artifact cannot be sacrificed
Yes, tap it for mana, then sacrifice it to the ability
No, it only pays for spells
exercises.explanation: Heartwood can supply the one mana and then be sacrificed as the other cost. Keeping it available preserves this protection option.

twoHeadedGiant.intro: Playing a Two-Headed Giant prerelease? Build two decks from your shared pool, then plan each turn together. Start with these team rules and the Reality Fracture cards whose wording changes your decisions.

rules.title: One life total, two players
rules.text: Your team starts at 30 life and takes its turns together. Hands, mana, libraries, graveyards and control of permanents stay separate. You can discuss your hands and plans, but cannot spend your partner’s mana or activate their permanents.

rules.title: A free first mulligan for each player
rules.text: Each player’s first mulligan does not reduce their hand size. Decide keeps together: check what each hand contributes. The starting team skips its first draw step, so neither player on that team draws then.

rules.title: Read “each opponent” and “you” literally
rules.text: You have two opponents. An effect dealing 1 damage to each opponent normally reduces their team’s life by 2. “You gain 1 life” adds only 1 to your team’s total. Your partner gaining life does not mean you gained life for your own triggers.

rules.title: Plan one combat together
rules.text: Declare your team’s attackers together and specify which opponent or planeswalker each attacks. Either defending player’s creatures can block attackers aimed at their teammate, subject to normal blocking restrictions. Talk through removal and tricks before declaring attacks; check both opponents’ available mana.

rules.title: Your partner’s board is not yours
rules.text: “Target creature” can include your partner’s creature if it is otherwise a legal target. “Target creature you control” cannot. Empower uses your Jace tokens, threshold counts your graveyard, and a bonus to creatures you control does not boost your partner’s army.

cards.note: With a legal target when it resolves and no prevention or replacement effects, it exiles one creature or planeswalker, deals 1 to each opponent (2 off their team total), and gains you 1 life. The life gain is not doubled.
Its entry trigger makes each opponent discard one card. That can take two cards from the opposing team, but an opponent with an empty hand cannot discard.
Its attack trigger deals 1 to each opponent and gains you 1 life even if it is later blocked. Count that separately from combat damage; prevention can still change the result.
Can give your partner’s creature +2/+2 and flying. You still empower your own Jace token, not theirs. Agree on the attack before spending the trick.
Its protection target and your fighter must be permanents or creatures you control. It cannot protect your partner’s creature or use that creature as your fighter.
Your scry or surveil triggers its bonus once each turn, affecting only creatures you control. Your partner’s surveil does not trigger it and their attackers do not receive the bonus.
The −2 makes every player sacrifice a creature, including your partner. Only you create the Beast, and only if you sacrificed a creature this way. Discuss your partner’s loss before activating.

exercises.question: Both teams are at 30. Your Extended Absence resolves with a legal target. No effects change damage or life gain. What are the new life totals?
options: Your team 31; opposing team 28
Your team 32; opposing team 28
Your team 31; opposing team 29
exercises.explanation: Each opponent takes 1 damage, reducing their shared total by 2. Only you gain 1 life, adding 1 to your team total.

exercises.question: Your partner controls a creature with no targeting restrictions. Can your Academic Ascent target it?
options: No, only your creatures
Yes; you empower your own Jace
Yes; your partner also gets the empower
exercises.explanation: The target says “creature”, without “you control”. The spell’s controller still performs empower using their own Jace tokens.

exercises.question: An opponent targets your partner’s creature with removal. Can your Vigorbloom Charm’s protection mode target that creature?
options: Yes, because you share a turn
No, you do not control it
exercises.explanation: The protection mode requires a permanent you control. Being teammates does not share control of permanents.

exercises.question: A ground creature attacks your partner. You control an untapped Rank Rat. No effects restrict blocking. Can your Rat block that attacker?
options: Yes
No, only your partner can block
exercises.explanation: The defending team blocks together. Your creatures can block attackers aimed at your teammate when normal blocking requirements are met.

exercises.question: You control Prudent Fateseer. Only your partner surveils, and nothing else relevant happens. Does your Fateseer trigger?
options: Yes, and it boosts both armies
Yes, but only your creatures
No
exercises.explanation: Its trigger says “you scry or surveil”. Your partner is a different player. Even when you trigger it yourself, only creatures you control get the bonus.

decisions.title: Check the support
decisions.question: Your green deck has Titanbones but no repeatable lifegain. Which discovery in the rest of your pool most directly improves its case for inclusion?
options: Another expensive creature with no lifegain
Greenhouse Propagator and several creatures to follow it
A single card that gains life but does nothing else
reasoning: More expensive creatures do not supply the trigger Titanbones needs, and compete for space at the top of the curve.
Propagator can gain life as creatures enter, repeatedly growing Titanbones while also contributing mana. You still need to cast and keep both creatures in play.
One isolated lifegain spell is less reliable support and may cost a card without improving your board. Look for useful cards that enable the payoff through normal play.
decisions.explanation: Propagator can gain life as creatures enter, repeatedly growing Titanbones while also contributing mana. You still need to cast and keep both creatures in play.

decisions.title: Count the payoff
decisions.question: Bloombrute already drew you a card from Greenhouse Propagator this turn. You can cast Seed Suture now, but do not need its counter for this combat. Will casting it now produce a second Bloombrute draw?
options: Yes, every lifegain event draws
No; the counter and life still happen, but Bloombrute has already triggered this turn
No, so the spell cannot be cast
reasoning: Bloombrute is limited to one draw trigger each turn, even if separate spells or abilities gain life.
The spell remains useful for its counter and life, but saving it for another legal casting opportunity may allow a fresh Bloombrute trigger. Do not count a second draw this turn.
The once-per-turn restriction belongs to Bloombrute, not to Seed Suture. You can cast the spell normally.
decisions.explanation: The spell remains useful for its counter and life, but saving it for another legal casting opportunity may allow a fresh Bloombrute trigger. Do not count a second draw this turn.

decisions.title: Plan the mana
decisions.question: You have two untapped Forests and an untapped Heartwood Crafter that can tap. Which three-mana play can its mana help pay for?
options: A three-mana creature spell from your hand
The Crafter’s prepared Soul Tether
Any green spell, regardless of where you cast it
reasoning: The mana cannot be spent to cast a spell from your hand. Treating this as an ordinary mana creature leads to incorrect curves.
A prepared spell is cast as a copy from outside your hand, so the restricted mana can pay its generic cost. Soul Tether then supplies a normal red-green mana source.
The restriction is about casting from hand, not the colour of the spell. The two Forests must still supply any required coloured mana.
decisions.explanation: A prepared spell is cast as a copy from outside your hand, so the restricted mana can pay its generic cost. Soul Tether then supplies a normal red-green mana source.

decisions.title: Keep an engine online
decisions.question: You have exactly seven cards in your graveyard and want Theorix Metamage to attack in the air. Before declaring attackers, you can exile a graveyard card for an unrelated effect. What should you check?
options: Threshold stays on once reached
Whether the exiled card is a creature; only creatures count
Whether you can return to seven cards before relying on flying
reasoning: Threshold is continuously checked, not permanently unlocked. Dropping to six removes the bonus.
All cards count toward threshold. Exiling any one of the seven drops the total to six.
Graveyard resources compete with threshold. At six cards the Metamage loses flying and its power bonus; count the resulting graveyard before planning the attack.
decisions.explanation: Graveyard resources compete with threshold. At six cards the Metamage loses flying and its power bonus; count the resulting graveyard before planning the attack.

decisions.title: Evaluate what removal leaves
decisions.question: Your opponent casts Kiora and gets a Dragon. You can then put Memory Trap on Kiora. What does that answer leave behind?
options: The existing Dragon remains, but Kiora cannot use its Dragon-making ability while trapped
The Dragon disappears when Kiora loses abilities
Memory Trap reverses Kiora’s arrival trigger
reasoning: Memory Trap shuts down future use of Kiora’s abilities. It does not remove the separate token already created, which is why arrival value makes a threat harder to answer completely.
The Dragon is an independent token, not something that lasts only while Kiora has abilities.
An already-resolved arrival trigger is not undone by later removing abilities. You still need a plan for the Dragon.
decisions.explanation: Memory Trap shuts down future use of Kiora’s abilities. It does not remove the separate token already created, which is why arrival value makes a threat harder to answer completely.

decisions.title: Use the sideboard
decisions.question: After game one, you have seen only blue and black creatures and planeswalkers from your opponent. What is the reason to leave Flourishing Grapple out unless new information changes the matchup?
options: It cannot deal damage in Limited
None of the observed threats are eligible red or white targets
Sideboard cards cannot be changed between games
reasoning: It can deal damage, but only with the required creatures and an eligible opposing target.
Its colour restriction matters more than its cheap cost. Against the threats you have actually seen, it has no legal opposing target; reassess if a red or white threat appears.
Sealed sideboarding lets you adapt between games. The issue is the card’s suitability for this opponent, not a ban on changing your deck.
decisions.explanation: Its colour restriction matters more than its cheap cost. Against the threats you have actually seen, it has no legal opposing target; reassess if a red or white threat appears.

decisions.title: Budget turns as well as counters
decisions.question: You cast Way of the Healer and create a new Jace token with five loyalty. You use its granted minus-two ability to make a Cadet. Can you also use that Jace to draw a card this turn?
options: Yes, because three loyalty remains
Yes, because the two abilities have different names
No; that planeswalker has already used a loyalty ability this turn
reasoning: Enough counters pay the cost, but do not override the one-loyalty-activation-per-turn limit.
Different loyalty abilities still share the same activation limit for that planeswalker.
You must wait for a later legal activation opportunity. Protecting the Jace is part of receiving the remaining value; the enchantment does not supply every benefit immediately.
decisions.explanation: You must wait for a later legal activation opportunity. Protecting the Jace is part of receiving the remaining value; the enchantment does not supply every benefit immediately.

decisions.title: Notice removal’s dependency
decisions.question: You need Compel Brutality to kill an opposing creature using your only creature’s power. The opponent has mana open and a removal spell could kill your creature in response. What is the risk?
options: The damage is guaranteed once you choose the mode
The spell needs your chosen creature to remain available to deal damage
The opponent cannot respond because this is your turn
reasoning: Choosing a mode does not lock in guaranteed damage from a creature that is removed before resolution.
If your creature is gone, it cannot deal this damage. Consider whether you can protect the source, choose the planeswalker mode if available, or wait for a safer window.
Players can normally respond to spells on either player’s turn; sorcery timing does not prevent responses.
decisions.explanation: If your creature is gone, it cannot deal this damage. Consider whether you can protect the source, choose the planeswalker mode if available, or wait for a safer window.

decisions.title: Check your own deck too
decisions.question: The opponent has strong creature arrival triggers, so you consider Karn, Argent Defender. Your deck also relies on empower arrival triggers. What is the key tradeoff?
options: Karn stops only opposing triggers
Your own empower arrival triggers also stop while Karn is present
Karn prevents every creature from entering prepared
reasoning: Karn’s restriction applies to the battlefield, not only the opponent’s cards.
The sideboard effect is symmetrical. Weigh the opponent’s lost value against your own; entering prepared itself is not a triggered ability and is not stopped.
Entering prepared is not a triggered ability. Distinguish that wording from abilities beginning with when or whenever.
decisions.explanation: The sideboard effect is symmetrical. Weigh the opponent’s lost value against your own; entering prepared itself is not a triggered ability and is not stopped.

decisions.title: Read the exception precisely
decisions.question: Ajani Unrelenting is in play. Both players have Cadets, and you have a nontoken creature with three toughness and no other protection. What does Ajani’s minus-three do to those creatures?
options: Spare all tokens and damage only nontoken creatures
Spare your Cadets, but deal four to opposing Cadets and your nontoken creature
Spare all of your creatures
reasoning: The exception is tokens you control, not every token on the battlefield.
Your Cadets are exempt. Opposing tokens and your own nontoken creatures take the damage, so plan the sweep around the actual survivors.
Your nontoken creatures are not exempt. The card can produce a favourable sweep without being completely one-sided.
decisions.explanation: Your Cadets are exempt. Opposing tokens and your own nontoken creatures take the damage, so plan the sweep around the actual survivors.
